# Chapter 5 — Zero Trust Across Vendors

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
Zero Trust architectures stall in mixed estates for a reason nobody puts on the slide: every enforcement surface speaks its own dialect of "who is this," and policy authored in five dialects is five policies. This chapter makes the series' central argument — that the codebook facet is the policy subject those dialects can all evaluate — and follows a single predicate as it compiles into the native membership construct of each surface. It then closes the loop that gives the architecture its verb: typed drift findings as the continuous verification that the subject itself is still trustworthy.
:::

## The Missing Noun

Zero Trust is usually explained by its verbs — verify explicitly, grant least privilege, assume breach — and the verbs are sound. What mixed estates lack is the noun. *Verify* what, exactly? A microsegmentation rule needs a subject: the set of machines belonging to cyber-operations, the contractors, the privileged accounts inside a division. Each enforcement surface offers its own way to express such a set — and none of them agrees with the others. An NSX group is not a Palo Alto dynamic address group is not a cloud security group is not an Entra dynamic-membership rule. An enterprise that authors "contractor workloads may not reach the finance segment" five times, in five grammars, against five differently-spelled notions of *contractor*, does not have one policy enforced five ways. It has five policies that resemble each other on a good day, drifting apart on every other day.

The substrate's answer is to supply the noun. A facet predicate — department is IT, and classification is Contractor, and account type is Service — is a boolean expression over codebook facets. It mentions no vendor, because facets are profile-agnostic by construction: the previous three chapters stamped the same facets onto Entra objects, Okta profiles, LDAP entries, cloud workloads, and NSX-tagged virtual machines. The predicate is authored once, against the only vocabulary in the estate that is governed, versioned, and drift-checked.

> The predicate is the unit of authoring. The profile is the unit of projection. No enforcement surface owns the subject; every enforcement surface evaluates it.

## One Predicate, Many Compilations

What happens to the predicate next is compilation, and the target grammar varies by surface while the meaning does not. On NSX, the predicate becomes a security group whose membership criteria match the facet tags the VMware profile stamped — and the distributed firewall consumes the group directly. On a Palo Alto estate, the same predicate becomes a dynamic address group keyed on registered tags, the construct that platform's rules already target. Elisity evaluates it as a policy group over the identity and asset attributes it ingests from the directories the substrate stamps. On AWS and Google Cloud, the predicate scopes security groups and firewall rules through resource tags and secure tags — the workload-plane facets of chapter three, doing double duty as enforcement inputs. And on the Microsoft estate it is the construct the OrgPath series spent chapters on: a dynamic-group membership rule over extension attributes, feeding Conditional Access.

The compilation targets differ in expressiveness, and an honest architecture says so: a tag-membership grammar cannot express everything a directory query can, and the projection holds itself to the subset every target evaluates faithfully. What matters is that the *subject* never forks. When the codebook deprecates a division and the governed change replaces its value, the predicate's meaning updates at the root, and every compiled projection follows on its next evaluation — because every projection reads facets, and the facets are reconciled to the codebook.

It is worth a sentence on what this does to least privilege, because entitlement sprawl is where most programs bleed. The grammar that scopes a firewall segment is the same grammar that scopes an access package, a delegation boundary, or a recertification campaign: a facet predicate. An entitlement scoped to engineers in cyber-operations is one predicate, not one group per system per quarter — and the access review that certifies it reasons over the same governed facets the drift engine validates. The reviewer and the firewall are finally reading the same sentence.

## Continuous Verification, Made Specific

Zero Trust's most repeated phrase — continuously verify — is also its least operationalized. Verify against what, on what cadence, with what consequence? The substrate gives the phrase a definition it can keep. The drift engine already walks every stamped surface on a schedule and classifies divergence by type: a facet value outside the codebook, a deprecated value still in service, a facet absent where the profile binds it, an overflow casualty never captured at all. In a single-vendor estate those findings were governance hygiene. In the architecture this chapter describes they are something sharper: a drifted facet is a *policy subject that can no longer be trusted*, because every compiled projection downstream of it is now evaluating stale or invalid input.

That reframing earns drift a place in the enforcement loop rather than the audit binder. A workload whose facets have drifted is a workload whose segmentation assignment is suspect — flag it, fence it, or at minimum surface it with the severity its blast radius implies. And the cross-profile case sharpens the point further: the same subject is often stamped on two surfaces at once — an identity in the directory, its workload in vSphere — and the planes can disagree. Cross-profile divergence is its own typed finding, because two surfaces disagreeing about a machine's department is not a data-quality nuisance; it is two firewalls enforcing two different opinions about the same asset.

Mapped against the maturity model language federal and commercial programs both borrow — the CISA pillars of identity, devices, networks, applications, and data, with visibility and governance running across them — the substrate's contribution is the same at every pillar: a common, governed, continuously verified subject underneath controls that previously each invented their own. The pillars stop being five programs with five vocabularies.

What remains is the practical question every architecture chapter defers: how an enterprise actually gets there from here, without replacing the platforms it already runs. That is the final chapter.
